catalog_quote: [p.65] ... comment doit-on interpréter leur jeu dans les dissyllabes kagoro ? Dans les dissyllabes de la classe H, la première syllabe prédomine en ce qui concerne la hauteur tonale et l'intensité. Dans les rares cas où la prédominance d'intensité n'est pas évidente, la première syllabe a une durée nettement supérieure. Dans les dissyllabes de la classe A, la deuxième syllabe prédomine en hauteur ... [p.66] l'accent, dont les composantes diffèrent. Dans les mots H, il est formé par la hauteur tonale et par l'intensité, tandis que dans les mots A, par la hauteur tonale et la durée. Cette tendance est moins évidente dans les mots de la classe H ayant une voyelle nasale dans la deuxième syllabe et dans les mots de la classe A ayant une voyelle nasale dans dans la première syllabe. Il est sans doute trop tôt pour classer le kagoro de Sébékoro en langues à accent, mais il est évident qu'il évolue dans cette direction. Il est intéressant de comparer le cas du kagoro avec la situation en mandinka où, d'après D. Creissels [1982], un système à accent se développe sur la base d'un système tonal typique pour les langues manding. Seulement, le résulat est juste le contraire de ce qu'on observe en kagoro: en mandinka, les mots de la classe H ont l'accent sur la deuxième syllabe, et les mots de la classe A l'ont sur la première.

new_statements.translation: [p.65] In class-H disyllables the first syllable predominates as regards pitch and intensity. In the rare cases where the predominance of intensity is not evident, the first syllable has a clearly greater duration. In class-A disyllables the second syllable predominates in pitch ... [p.66] ... the accent, whose components differ: in H words it is formed by pitch and intensity, whereas in A words by pitch and duration. [...] It is doubtless too early to class the Kagoro of Sébékoro among accent languages, but it is evident that it is evolving in that direction.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kagoro is a two-tone Manding language with word-level lexical tonal classes H (high) and A (rising/low). Vydrine's instrumental data (Sébékoro) show an emergent accent-like prominence whose position is determined by tonal class, not by a fixed edge: first syllable prominent (pitch+intensity) in class-H disyllables, second syllable prominent (pitch+duration) in class-A disyllables. He explicitly declines to classify Kagoro as an accent language yet ('too early') while saying it is evolving that way, the mirror image of Mandinka (Creissels 1982: class-H words accented on the 2nd syllable). In JWAL 2004:114 he states that in 'some Kagoro dialects' the tone-to-accent transformation has occurred. No source gives a fixed stress position.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in the accessible snippets.
new_statements.exceptions: p.66: the tendency is less evident in class-H words with a nasal vowel in the second syllable and class-A words with a nasal vowel in the first syllable; p.65 compensation when V2 is very short or final nasal vowel; p.101 in survey wordlists from other villages an intensity accent is marked per word only 'là où [il] est nettement distinguable'.
new_statements.domain_note: Citation forms of mono- and disyllabic nouns recorded from one main Sébékoro informant (10 days fieldwork, 1998; other informants 'occasionnellement'); tone domain is the word, not the syllable (p.53). Access caveat: text seen only through Google Books snippet view (overlapping page-numbered snippets, saved verbatim); the full pages 62-67 were not read.
new_statements.identity_note: Vydrine 2001's phonology/tone chapter describes the Kagoro of Sébékoro (western Kagoro zone, Kaarta, Mali; one principal informant, 1998), with survey wordlists from other Kagoro villages (p.101); Creissels 1986 describes the Kagoro of Kourougué near Diéma; Vydrine 2004 restricts the completed tone-to-accent shift to 'some Kagoro dialects'. All fall under kago1248 (Kagoro/Kakolo, ISO xkg); Glottolog has no dialect-level codes. Western Kagoro forms a continuum with the Bage dialect of Kita Maninka (Vydrin 2017: 17-18).

new_statements.quote: В некоторых северо-западных манден проявляется тенденция к формированию, на фоне тоновых противопоставлений, динамического ударения. Начало такого процесса можно проследить в кагоро [Vydrine 2001]; более продвинутая стадия становления ударения описана Дени Кресельсом для мандинка [Creissels 1982a]. В мандинка этот процесс вызвал кардинальную перестройку всей просодической системы, отличия которой от тональных систем типа бамана весьма значительны.
new_statements.translation: In some north-western Manding varieties a tendency toward the formation of a dynamic stress, against the background of the tonal oppositions, is manifested. The beginning of such a process can be traced in Kagoro [Vydrine 2001]; a more advanced stage of the establishment of stress is described by Denis Creissels for Mandinka [Creissels 1982a]. In Mandinka this process caused a radical restructuring of the whole prosodic system, whose differences from tonal systems of the Bamana type are very considerable.

new_statements.relation_note: Same picture as the existing statement from Vydrine 2001 (tone language with an incipient, tonal-class-dependent accent): the 2003 survey calls it the beginning of a tendency toward dynamic stress in Kagoro, citing Vydrine 2001, and adds no placement rule, so it neither refines nor contradicts the p.65-66 statement (H-class disyllables prominent on the 1st syllable, A-class on the 2nd). The catalog record for Kagoro has an empty rule field; this work supports keeping it as 'tonal, with a stress statement / incipient stress, no fixed position' rather than any fixed placement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kagoro is a two-tone Manding language (two tonemes, H and L-H, with the word as the tonal domain, p. 97) in which a dynamic (intensity) stress is only beginning to form on top of the tonal oppositions; the article gives no rule for where that stress falls and refers the compiler to Vydrine 2001 for the details.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the article says only that the process is at its beginning in Kagoro and more advanced in Mandinka. The conclusion (pp. 109-110) names only Mandinka as the Manding case where the system may turn accentual, and states that stress coexisting with tone is attested in Mande (Guro, Kpelle, possibly Bobo and San).
new_statements.identity_note: Vydrin 2003 speaks of Kagoro as a whole, citing Vydrine 2001, whose instrumental accent study is of the Sebekoro variety; the 2003 survey does not name a dialect.

tone_statements.quote: 2.1.3.4.2. В подавляющем большинстве западных языков манде представлены только две тонемы, что может интерпретироваться и как противопоставление одной маркированной тонемы (обычно низкотоновой) её отсутствию ... На северной периферии наблюдается ослабление тоновых противопоставлений: их нейтрализация в некоторых позициях ведёт к повышению роли словесного ударения (что отмечено в языках мандинка [Creissels 1982b] и кагоро [Vydrine 2001], причём в обоих языках это развитие идёт в разных направлениях)...
tone_statements.translation: 2.1.3.4.2. In the overwhelming majority of Western Mande languages only two tonemes are present, which can also be interpreted as the opposition of one marked toneme (usually the low one) to its absence ... On the northern periphery a weakening of tonal oppositions is observed: their neutralisation in some positions leads to an increased role of word stress (noted in Mandinka [Creissels 1982b] and Kagoro [Vydrine 2001], the development going in different directions in the two languages)...
tone_statements.summary: Comparative work: Kagoro in the two-toneme W. Mande group, with weakening tone contrasts and growing word stress; own F0 data: low-toned nasal prefix, initial tone lowering. Count/TBU group-level only.
